case_title: Raju Devade v. State of Maharashtra
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour; former romantic partner (love affair). The victim had asked the accused to marry her.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (case initially registered under IPC s.307); Evidence Act 1872 s.32 (dying declarations)
weapon: Kerosene oil and a burning match-stick
evidence_type: Dying declarations (police-recorded oral statement treated as dying declaration; Executive Magistrate's dying declaration; a later Executive Magistrate's statement); brother's evidence (PW 4); medical evidence (autopsy, about 72 per cent burns)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302; sentenced to life imprisonment
neutral_facts: The victim, an 18-year-old, was alone at home in the late evening on 4 March 1989. The victim's parents had gone out, and the victim's brother and sister had gone to watch an evening movie. At about 9.30 pm the brother returned and found the victim on fire in bushes near the house. He smothered the flames with a quilt and took the victim on a push-cart to the Rural Hospital, where no doctor was available. A waterman and a maid-servant cleaned the wounds and administered intravenous saline. A police sub-inspector arrived at once and recorded an oral statement from the victim, which bore the victim's thumb impression. In it the victim said the accused, with whom the victim had a love affair and who the victim said had made the victim pregnant, had been asked to marry the victim that evening. The victim said the accused then poured kerosene on the victim and set the victim alight with a match-stick. On the police requisition, an Executive Magistrate recorded a dying declaration at the hospital in the presence of two hospital employees, and the victim put a thumb impression on it. The victim was then moved to a district hospital. On 5 March 1989 another Executive Magistrate recorded a different statement, attributing the burns to a falling chimney lamp while the victim slept. That statement had no thumb impression. The victim died on 9 March 1989. A medical officer conducted the autopsy and recorded about 72 per cent burns. The defence case was that the burns were accidental.
physical_harm: Death from burn injuries (about 72 per cent burns); victim died 9 March 1989
motive: Accused's unwillingness to marry the pregnant victim after a love affair, after the victim repeatedly asked him to marry her (accepted from PW 4's evidence and the dying declarations)
key_evidence_accepted: Police-recorded oral statement and the Executive Magistrate's dying declaration (same account, implicating the accused); PW 4's evidence on the motive; autopsy and doctor's evidence that death was from burns; rejection of the chimney-accident theory
witness_credibility: Court accepted that the police sub-inspector had no reason to implicate the accused; accepted PW 4's evidence on motive; did not expressly assess PW 5's non-support of the panchnama
trial_duration: offence: 04.03.1989; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 13.04.2007; Supreme Court: 29.06.2016
legal_representation: Appellant: Kumar Parimal and Ms. Praveena Gautam (Advocates). State/respondents: Nishant Ramakantrao Katneshwarkar (Advocate).
investigation_status: FIR (case No. 63/89) registered; oral statement recorded; Executive Magistrate requisitioned; seven prosecution witnesses and one defence witness; trial completed; charge converted to s.302 IPC
procedural_irregularity: First dying declaration recorded without a doctor's certificate; Rural Hospital had no trained medical staff; third dying declaration not in question-answer form and lacked thumb impression. Court held none of these fatal.
appeal_history: Trial court (Sessions Judge): convicted under s.302 IPC, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction maintained (13.04.2007). Supreme Court: appeal dismissed.
prosecution_argument: State supported the High Court and Sessions Judge: the first two dying declarations were properly relied on with cogent reasons, and there were valid reasons for rejecting the third.
defence_argument: Inconsistent dying declarations required caution; the third declaration exonerated the accused; PW 4 was an interested witness with contradictions and omissions; no independent witness; the victim could not give the accused's surname; the death was accidental (falling chimney lamp); PW 5 did not support the panchnama; the marriage claim conflicted with PW 4.
legal_principle_applied: Each dying declaration must be considered independently on its own merit and cannot be rejected because of the contents of another; the court must decide which reflects the true state of affairs. Non-question-answer form does not by itself defeat reliability. Where declarations conflict, the court looks for corroboration and may lean toward the first.
precedent_relied_upon: Bhupan v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 2002 (2) SCC 556; State of Punjab v. Parveen Kumar, 2005 (9) SCC 769; Sudhakar v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 2012 (7) SCC 569; Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab, 2006 (13) SCC 130; Prem Kumar Gulati v. State of Haryana, 2014 (14) SCC 646; Nallam Veera Stayanarayana v. Public Prosecutor (cited in Sudhakar, as quoted in the judgment)
